hook.text: The Bay of Pigs invasion was approved by brilliant advisors who privately had doubts—but said nothing.

buildup.text: Irving Janis coined 'groupthink': when cohesive groups prioritize harmony over honest evaluation.

discovery.text: Symptoms include illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, and pressure on dissenters to conform.

twist.text: The group doesn't suppress dissent on purpose. Members genuinely believe the group can't be wrong.

climax.text: NASA's Challenger disaster is another case: engineers warned about O-ring failure, but group pressure silenced them.

punchline.text: The smarter the group, the more dangerous its silence.

quiz.question: What is groupthink?
options: Groups prioritizing harmony over critical thinking
Thinking as an individual in a group

details.summary: Groupthink occurs when desire for group harmony overrides realistic evaluation of alternatives. Janis identified it in failures like the Bay of Pigs invasion. Symptoms include illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, and pressure on dissenters.
details.whyItMatters: Groupthink explains catastrophic collective decisions. Recognizing its symptoms enables teams to build structures that protect critical thinking within groups.
takeaways: Groups suppress dissent in pursuit of consensus
Illusion of invulnerability leads to excessive risk-taking
Structured devil's advocacy can counteract groupthink

faq.question: What are the main symptoms of groupthink?
faq.answer: Illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalization, stereotyping of out-groups, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters, illusion of unanimity, and self-appointed mindguards who shield the group from dissenting information. These symptoms reinforce each other in a feedback loop.

faq.question: How can organizations prevent groupthink?
faq.answer: Assign a devil's advocate role. Invite outside experts. Leaders should withhold their opinion initially to avoid anchoring. Encourage anonymous feedback mechanisms. Create subgroups that work independently on the same problem. Normalize constructive disagreement as a team value.
